stem: A 32-year-old woman fractures the shaft of her femur. The dense bone forming the walls of the shaft, which resists compressive forces, is organized into which of the following structural units?

options.label: A
options.misconception: The spongy architecture is being assigned to the dense shaft.
options.explanation: Spongy (cancellous) bone has open spaces and supports shifts in weight distribution; it fills the epiphyses, not the dense diaphyseal walls.

options.label: B
options.misconception: None; the osteon (Haversian system) is the unit of compact bone.
options.explanation: Compact bone's microscopic structural unit is the osteon, or Haversian system: concentric rings of calcified matrix (lamellae) around a central canal; compact bone is dense and withstands compressive forces.

options.label: C
options.misconception: A formative precursor is being cast as the load-bearing structure.
options.explanation: Osteoid is freshly secreted, not-yet-calcified matrix; it provides no compressive strength until mineralized.

options.label: D
options.misconception: A cartilaginous joint is being cast as a bone tissue.
options.explanation: A synchondrosis joins bones with hyaline cartilage (e.g. the epiphyseal plate); it is a joint, not a structural unit of compact bone.

options.label: E
options.misconception: A developmental scaffold is being cast as the mature shaft unit.
options.explanation: The periosteal collar is an early ossification structure around the fetal cartilage model; the mature diaphysis is built from osteons.

context: Learning objective: compact vs spongy bone. Compact bone (diaphyseal walls, under the periosteum) is dense and resists compression; its unit is the osteon — concentric lamellae around a central (Haversian) canal. Spongy (cancellous) bone has open trabecular spaces and fills epiphyses and flat bones.
